Build a Higher-Order Network (HON)

Source: R/hon.R
build_hon.Rd

build_hon() builds a higher-order network from sequences with the BuildHON algorithm (Xu, Wickramarathne & Chawla, 2016) or its faster variant BuildHON+ (Saebi et al., 2020), and returns a net_hon. A node is a state together with as much of its preceding history as changes where the sequence goes next: "B" is a first-order node, and "A -> B" is state B reached from A, kept as a node of its own when the distribution of the next state after A then B differs enough from the one after B alone (see Details), or when it begins a longer history that is kept, such as "A -> B -> C". It reads sequences in a wide data frame or character matrix, a list of state vectors, or a netobject, cograph_network or tna built from sequences.

An edge weight is the probability of moving from the source node to the target node. A higher-order node marks a dependence on earlier states that a first-order network, with one node per state, averages away. Whether a history is extended is decided by a rule, not a test: the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the longer and the shorter history's next-state distributions must exceed a threshold that grows with the order and shrinks with how often the longer history was observed, so the same divergence passes more easily for a history observed more often, and nodes resting on a few observations are noisy (raise min_freq to set them aside). To test whether the sequences need memory beyond the first order, use markov_order_test(); build_mogen() selects an order by likelihood, and pathways() lists the higher-order paths found here.

Usage

build_hon(
  data,
  max_order = 5L,
  min_freq = 1L,
  collapse_repeats = FALSE,
  method = "hon+"
)

# S3 method for class 'net_hon'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_hon'
summary(object, ...)

Arguments

data

The sequences. A data frame or character matrix has one row per sequence and one column per position; a data frame of several columns must hold only position columns named as a numbered run (T1, T2, ...), or be a sequence table returned by a Nestimate verb such as extract_sequences(), and any other frame raises an error of class nestimate_bad_input (declare its positions with build_network(state_cols = ) and pass the network). A plain list holds one vector of states per sequence. A netobject, a bare cograph_network or a tna built from sequences contributes its stored sequences, with a tna's numeric state codes converted to their labels. Values are read as character. A missing value ends a run of observed states, so a sequence with an internal gap becomes two sequences, and sequences with fewer than two states are dropped; when none is left, an error is raised. A one-hot or association network, a netobject_group, a classed list, and a matrix or data frame of only 0 and 1 raise an error of class nestimate_bad_input.

max_order

The highest order a node may reach, that is, how many states of history it carries. Default 5. Lower orders result where the data do not support a longer history; print() reports the highest order reached beside the one requested. Must be at least 1; a fractional value is truncated to a whole number.

min_freq

The minimum count for a transition to be used. Transitions observed fewer than min_freq times are treated as zero, also in the totals that set the divergence threshold. Default 1. Must be at least 1; a fractional value is truncated to a whole number.

collapse_repeats

Whether to collapse each run of a repeated state into one state before counting (after splitting at missing values). Default FALSE.

method

The algorithm. "hon+" (default) is BuildHON+, which counts a longer history only when it is needed and skips an extension when even the largest divergence the history could reach would not pass the threshold. "hon" is the original BuildHON, which first counts the transitions from every history of up to max_order states. Both stop at max_order.

x

For the print() method: a net_hon.

...

Ignored by the print() and summary() methods.

object

For the summary() method: a net_hon.

Value

A net_hon (class c("net_hon", "cograph_network")). Print it for the number of nodes, edges and sequences and the orders reached; summary() prints the same with the first-order states and the number of nodes of each order, and returns the network's edge table (integer from/to node indices and weight). extract_edges() gives the weight of each ordered pair of nodes by node name (pairs with zero weight are included at its default threshold = 0, and self-loops only with include_self = TRUE), pathways() the higher-order paths, build_honem() an embedding of the nodes and build_simplicial(type = "pathway") a simplicial complex; it draws with cograph::splot(). The print() method returns its input invisibly. The fields:

weights, matrix

The weighted adjacency matrix (rows are sources, columns targets) under two names: weights is the cograph_network field, matrix the higher-order name kept for compatibility. Rows and columns carry the node names in arrow notation (e.g. "A -> B").

ho_edges

The higher-order edge table, one row per edge: path (the full state sequence, e.g. "A -> B -> C"), from (the source node, its history), to (the next state), count (how often the transition was observed), probability (the transition probability), and from_order and to_order (the orders of the source and target nodes).

edges

The cograph_network edge table: one row per non-zero cell of weights, with integer from/to indices into nodes and a numeric weight. It is not the arrow-notation table, which is ho_edges.

nodes

A data frame with columns id, label and name, one row per node; label and name hold the node names in arrow notation.

n_nodes

The number of nodes.

n_edges

The number of rows of ho_edges.

first_order_states

The distinct states of the sequences analysed (after splitting at missing values, collapsing repeats and dropping short sequences), sorted.

max_order_requested

The max_order used.

max_order_observed

The highest order reached.

min_freq

The min_freq used.

n_trajectories

The number of sequences analysed, after splitting at missing values and dropping short ones.

directed

Always TRUE.

meta

The cograph_network metadata list (source, layout, and tna$method = "hon").

node_groups

Always NULL.

Details

Node names: a first-order node is the state itself, "A". A second-order node for "came from A, now at B" is "A -> B"; a third-order one is "A -> B -> C", and so on.

Algorithm:

  1. Count the transitions from every history of up to max_order states (subsequences of up to max_order + 1 states); BuildHON+ counts the longer histories only when they are needed.

  2. Turn the counts into next-state distributions, setting counts below min_freq to zero.

  3. For each first-order source, extend the history one state at a time and keep the longer history when the Kullback-Leibler divergence (base 2) of its distribution from the currently kept one exceeds order / log2(1 + n), where order is the new order and n the number of transitions counted from the longer history (after setting counts below min_freq to zero).

  4. Build the network from the kept histories, rewiring edges so the higher-order nodes are connected to each other.

The implementation follows the reference Python code of the two papers (pyHON and pyHON+).

References

Xu, J., Wickramarathne, T. L., & Chawla, N. V. (2016). Representing higher-order dependencies in networks. Science Advances, 2(5), e1600028.

Saebi, M., Xu, J., Kaplan, L. M., Ribeiro, B., & Chawla, N. V. (2020). Efficient modeling of higher-order dependencies in networks: from algorithm to application for anomaly detection. EPJ Data Science, 9(1), 15.

Examples

seqs <- list(c("A","B","C","D"), c("A","B","C","A"), c("B","C","D","A"))
hon <- build_hon(seqs, max_order = 2)

# \donttest{
# From list of trajectories
trajs <- list(
  c("A", "B", "C", "D", "A"),
  c("A", "B", "D", "C", "A"),
  c("A", "B", "C", "D", "A")
)
hon <- build_hon(trajs, max_order = 3, min_freq = 1)
print(hon)
#> Higher-Order Network (HON)
#>   Nodes:        4 (4 first-order states)
#>   Edges:        7
#>   Max order:    1 (requested 3)
#>   Min freq:     1
#>   Trajectories: 3
summary(hon)
#> Higher-Order Network (HON) Summary
#>   Nodes: 4 | Edges: 7 | Trajectories: 3
#>   First-order states: A, B, C, D
#>   Max order observed: 1 (requested: 3)
#>   Min frequency: 1
#>   Node order distribution:
#>     Order 1: 4 nodes
#>   from to    weight
#> 1    3  1 0.3333333
#> 2    4  1 0.6666667
#> 3    1  2 1.0000000
#> 4    2  3 0.6666667
#> 5    4  3 0.3333333
#> 6    2  4 0.3333333
#> 7    3  4 0.6666667

# From data.frame (rows = trajectories)
df <- data.frame(T1 = c("A", "A"), T2 = c("B", "B"),
                 T3 = c("C", "D"), T4 = c("D", "C"))
hon <- build_hon(df, max_order = 2)
# }
